see: 'VHF/UHF' printed on a TV antenna box or scanner
is: ITU band names: VHF is 30-300 MHz, UHF is 300-3,000 MHz
anchor: What do VHF and UHF stand for?

see: '2.4 GHz' or '6 GHz' on a Wi-Fi router box
is: The radio frequency the router transmits on, counted in hertz
anchor: What is a radio frequency, and what does "hertz" mean?

see: Full bars outside, one bar or none inside a building
is: Walls and especially energy-saving glass absorb or reflect signals, more so at higher frequencies
anchor: Why does my phone lose signal inside buildings?

see: A '5G UW' or '5G+' icon that vanishes when I walk indoors
is: Higher-frequency 5G carries more data but gets through walls poorly
anchor: Why do high frequencies carry more data?

see: Coverage map says good service but my phone struggles indoors
is: Outdoor maps do not capture building entry loss, which varies with construction
anchor: What is "building entry loss," and how do engineers model it?

see: A museum caption saying the Titanic created radio laws
is: The Radio Act of 1912 followed the Titanic and required radio licenses
anchor: Did the Titanic lead to radio laws?

see: A colorful US frequency allocation chart poster
is: NTIA's wall chart of the US Table of Frequency Allocations
anchor: What is the US frequency allocation chart?

see: 'This device complies with Part 15 of the FCC Rules' label
is: The device runs without a license, on condition it causes no harmful interference and accepts interference
anchor: What does "FCC Part 15" on my device mean?

see: Wi-Fi slows down when the microwave oven runs
is: Wi-Fi shares ISM bands, and Part 15 devices must accept interference from ISM equipment
anchor: What are ISM bands, and why do so many gadgets share them?

see: A router advertising Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7
is: Uses the 6 GHz band the FCC opened for unlicensed use in April 2020
anchor: What is 6 GHz Wi-Fi, and is it legal?

see: A news story about a carrier buying spectrum for billions
is: An FCC spectrum auction; licenses, not ownership, are sold
anchor: Why does the government auction airwaves?

see: Headlines about WRC-27
is: The 2027 ITU World Radiocommunication Conference in Shanghai, which revises the global radio treaty
anchor: When is the next World Radiocommunication Conference?

see: A car radio with AM and FM bands
is: Two broadcast bands: AM varies signal strength, FM varies frequency
anchor: What is the difference between AM and FM?

see: Far-away AM stations showing up at night
is: AM medium-wave signals can travel much farther after dark
anchor: What is the difference between AM and FM?

see: The stereo light flickering off on an FM station
is: A weak signal makes the radio drop the 38 kHz stereo subcarrier and go mono
anchor: How does FM carry stereo on one station?

see: An HD logo or HD2 channel on my car stereo
is: HD Radio, the US digital system riding alongside AM and FM stations
anchor: What is HD Radio, and what is DAB?

see: A DAB radio in the UK
is: Digital radio where many stations share one multiplex
anchor: What is HD Radio, and what is DAB?

see: My TV lost channels until I rescanned it
is: The 2017-2020 TV repack moved stations to new frequencies
anchor: Why did TV go digital, and why did I have to rescan my TV?

see: A NextGen TV logo on a new television
is: ATSC 3.0, the optional newer US broadcast TV standard
anchor: What is NextGen TV (ATSC 3.0), and is regular TV being shut off?

see: Tall lit towers along Route 128 in Needham
is: Boston's main TV transmitter sites, Cedar Street and Cabot Street
anchor: In Boston: what are the towers in Needham?

see: A tower with a wide triangular top holding several antennas
is: A candelabra tower carrying several TV stations at once
anchor: In Boston: what are the towers in Needham?

see: Bars on my phone changing as I walk
is: Your phone being served by, and handed off between, cell sites
anchor: How does a cell network work?

see: A 5G or LTE icon next to my signal bars
is: Which cellular generation your phone is using right now
anchor: What do 1G, 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G mean?

see: A canister or box on top of a light pole
is: Probably a small cell adding cellular capacity to a busy block
anchor: Is that a cell tower or a small cell?

see: Rows of rectangular panels at the top of a tall tower
is: A macro cell site covering a wide area
anchor: Is that a cell tower or a small cell?

see: My phone is much faster on some corners than others
is: Different 5G tiers: low band, mid band and short-range mmWave
anchor: What do low-band, mid-band and mmWave 5G mean?

see: News about 5G and airplane altimeters
is: The 2021-2022 FAA dispute over C-band 5G near airports
anchor: Why did 5G cause problems for airplanes?

see: Small antennas on subway tunnel walls
is: A distributed antenna system carrying cell signal underground
anchor: What is a DAS, and why is there signal in some tunnels?

see: Cell service on the T underground
is: The MBTA's tunnel DAS, in place since 2005 and upgraded for 5G
anchor: In Boston

see: My old phone or alarm panel stopped working in 2022
is: US carriers shut down their 3G networks in 2022 and January 2023
anchor: Why did my old phone stop working?

see: UK phone lost 3G
is: UK operators switched off 3G between 2023 and 2025
anchor: Elsewhere in the world

see: A radio clipped to a police officer's vest with a microphone on the shoulder
is: Land mobile radio, push-to-talk radio that works through repeaters
anchor: What is the radio on an officer's shoulder?

see: A scanner listing that says P25 Phase 1 or Phase 2
is: The digital public safety radio standard and its two versions
anchor: What is P25, and what does "Phase 2" mean?

see: Scanner audio that sounds digital and hops between frequencies
is: A trunked system, where a control channel assigns each conversation a free frequency
anchor: What is the radio on an officer's shoulder?

see: A rugged tablet or modem in an ambulance or police cruiser
is: Possibly FirstNet, the US first-responder broadband network on Band 14
anchor: What is FirstNet?

see: Scanner channels named BAPERN or MetroFire around Boston
is: Greater Boston's regional police and fire mutual aid radio on the T-Band
anchor: In Boston: what are BAPERN and the T-Band?

see: Radio chatter on 160-161 MHz near a rail line
is: Railroad VHF radio between crews and dispatchers
anchor: What is that chatter near the train tracks?

see: A harsh two-tone alarm interrupting TV or radio
is: The Emergency Alert System
anchor: What is the loud tone before an emergency message on TV or radio?

see: Every phone in a room blaring an alert at the same time
is: A Wireless Emergency Alert sent by cell broadcast
anchor: Why did every phone in the room go off at once?

see: A weather radio that sits silent then sounds an alarm
is: NOAA Weather Radio activated by SAME codes for your county
anchor: What is on 162.475 MHz?

see: A UK phone alert test on a Sunday afternoon
is: The UK Emergency Alerts system, first tested nationally April 23, 2023
anchor: Elsewhere in the world

see: A scanner for sale at an electronics store
is: Legal to own and use for unencrypted public radio in the US, with limits on sharing
anchor: Is it legal to own a police scanner in the US?

see: A Facebook group posting what's on the police scanner
is: Divulging scanner traffic, restricted by Section 705 but questioned after Bartnicki v. Vopper
anchor: Can I post or use what I hear on a scanner?

see: A gap in a scanner's frequency coverage labeled cellular
is: Federally required blocking of cellular frequencies
anchor: Why can't a scanner pick up cell phone calls?

see: A scanner mounted on a car dashboard
is: Restricted in some states, such as Florida and New York
anchor: Can I have a scanner in my car?

see: My scanner used to get local police and now it is silent
is: The agency went digital, moved to P25 Phase 2, or encrypted
anchor: Why did my scanner go quiet, and do I need a digital one?

see: Boston police missing from my scanner app
is: BPD encrypted on August 9, 2025, and offers a 5-minute delayed feed
anchor: In Boston: why can't I hear the police on my scanner?

see: A news story about police radio going dark
is: Police encryption, and the debate between officer safety and public access
anchor: Why are police departments encrypting their radios?

see: A UK scanner leaflet warning what you may listen to
is: Section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006
anchor: Elsewhere in the world

see: A flight tracker app showing a plane over my house
is: The plane's own ADS-B broadcast, picked up by volunteer ground receivers
anchor: What is ADS-B, and why can anyone receive it?

see: A plane labeled UAT or 978 on a tracking site
is: A US-only ADS-B link used mainly by small aircraft below 18,000 ft
anchor: What is the difference between 1090 and 978 ADS-B?

see: A plane on a tracker marked MLAT or with an estimated position
is: An aircraft with only a Mode S transponder, located by timing its replies at four or more receivers
anchor: What is MLAT, and why can't I see a plane on Flightradar24?

see: A plane I can hear but cannot find on Flightradar24
is: Too low for MLAT, outside receiver coverage, on 978 MHz, or blocked by its owner
anchor: What is MLAT, and why can't I see a plane on Flightradar24?

see: A private jet that shows up blank or not at all on a tracker
is: The owner has used the FAA's LADD blocking or a Privacy ICAO Address
anchor: Can owners hide a plane from flight trackers?

see: Military jets showing on one tracking site but not another
is: ADS-B Exchange describes itself as unfiltered, including military traffic
anchor: What is ADS-B Exchange?

see: Short digital bursts on a scanner around 129-131 MHz
is: ACARS, text messaging between aircraft and their airlines
anchor: What is ACARS?

see: Clipped voices on a scanner between 118 and 137 MHz
is: Air traffic control and pilots on the VHF airband
anchor: What frequency is air traffic control?

see: A website streaming live tower audio
is: Listening to aeronautical radio is permitted under US federal law; the UK is described as stricter
anchor: Is it legal to listen to air traffic control?

see: A transponder or squawk code mentioned in a flight tracker
is: The radar-reply box on the aircraft and the four-digit code ATC assigns
anchor: What does a transponder do?

see: Jets climbing in a steady line over Cambridge or Somerville
is: Runway 33L RNAV departures from Logan, concentrated on a narrow track since 2013-2014
anchor: In Boston: why do planes fly low over certain neighborhoods?

see: A ship app showing a ferry or tanker in the harbor
is: The vessel's AIS broadcast on 161.975/162.025 MHz, collected by shore receivers
anchor: What is AIS?

see: Big ships on a tracker but not small sailboats
is: SOLAS and US rules require AIS on larger and commercial vessels, not most recreational boats
anchor: Which ships have to carry AIS?

see: A tug or ferry showing on a ship tracker
is: US rules require Class A AIS on commercial vessels of 65 ft or more, larger towing vessels and big passenger vessels
anchor: What are the US rules for AIS?

see: A world map of ship icons that thins out at sea
is: MarineTraffic's network of coastal AIS receivers, mostly run by contributors
anchor: How does MarineTraffic track ships?

see: A marine radio or scanner tuned to channel 16
is: The international distress, safety and calling channel, 156.800 MHz
anchor: What is marine VHF channel 16?

see: A short data burst on marine channel 70
is: Digital Selective Calling, with no voice
anchor: What is marine VHF channel 16?

see: A handheld scanner at the waterfront picking up boats
is: Receiving marine radio is permitted under US federal law
anchor: Can I listen to marine radio?

see: A line of buoys in the water around Logan Airport
is: A 250-ft security zone marked by 29 buoys, set up in 2002
anchor: In Boston

see: A blue dot that drifts across the street downtown
is: GPS multipath and blocked satellites in an urban canyon
anchor: Why is my GPS wrong downtown?

see: A pale circle around my location dot
is: The phone's own estimate of its position error
anchor: How accurate is GPS on my phone?

see: A GPS test app showing satellites with different country flags
is: Your phone using GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou together
anchor: Is my phone using GPS, or something else?

see: Dual-frequency GPS (L1 + L5) on a phone spec sheet
is: A receiver using two GPS carriers to correct atmospheric delay
anchor: What frequencies does GPS use?

see: A small dome or puck antenna on a cell site
is: Possibly a GPS antenna; cell networks rely on GPS for precise timing
anchor: Why do cell towers and power grids need GPS?

see: A 'GPS privacy' plug-in device for sale online
is: A GPS jammer, which the FCC says has no lawful use in the US
anchor: Are GPS jammers illegal?

see: A plane on a flight tracker flying a strange zigzag near a border
is: Possible GNSS jamming or spoofing affecting its reported position
anchor: Why are planes losing GPS over the Baltic?

see: An 'atomic' clock with a tower icon that syncs overnight
is: A radio-controlled clock receiving NIST's WWVB on 60 kHz
anchor: How does an "atomic" clock set itself?

see: A ticking voice announcing Coordinated Universal Time on shortwave
is: NIST's WWV or WWVH time station
anchor: What is that ticking voice on shortwave?

see: Old tutorials for receiving NOAA weather images on 137 MHz
is: NOAA APT, shut down in 2025
anchor: Can I still pick up NOAA weather satellite pictures?

see: A cloud loop of all North America on the TV forecast
is: Imagery from NOAA's geostationary GOES satellites
anchor: What is GOES, and why does it never move?

see: A bright steady light crossing the sky in a few minutes
is: Often the International Space Station
anchor: Can I hear the International Space Station?

see: Smeared pictures with 'ARISS' in the corner posted online
is: SSTV images received from the ISS on 145.800 MHz
anchor: What is SSTV from the ISS, and how do people receive it?

see: A line of satellites moving together after sunset
is: Starlink satellites
anchor: How many Starlink satellites are there?

see: A flat white Starlink dish on a roof or RV
is: A Starlink user terminal using Ku/Ka-band links
anchor: What frequencies does Starlink use?

see: My phone shows 'SAT' with no bars
is: Direct-to-cell satellite texting, such as T-Mobile T-Satellite
anchor: How can my phone text from space?

see: "This device must accept any interference received" in a gadget manual
is: The FCC Part 15 condition for unlicensed radios: no protected frequency, no harmful interference allowed.
anchor: What does "must accept any interference received" mean?

see: Wi-Fi cuts out when the microwave is running
is: The oven leaks 2.45 GHz energy into 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channels 7-11.
anchor: Why does my Wi-Fi drop when the microwave is on?

see: A router box labeled Wi-Fi 6, 6E or 7
is: Wi-Fi Alliance generation names for IEEE 802.11ax and 802.11be.
anchor: What do Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6 and 7 mean?

see: My router shows separate 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz networks
is: Three unlicensed bands with different range and capacity trade-offs.
anchor: Why does my router have 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands?

see: My phone shows no 6 GHz Wi-Fi while traveling in Europe
is: The EU opened only the lower part of the 6 GHz band.
anchor: Can I use 6 GHz Wi-Fi outside the US?

see: The blue angular Bluetooth "B" logo
is: Runic-style branding for a 2.4 GHz short-range radio named after a Danish king.
anchor: Why is Bluetooth called Bluetooth?

see: A store app that knows which aisle I am in
is: A BLE beacon broadcasting an ID that the app recognizes.
anchor: What is a Bluetooth beacon?

see: A Matter, Thread, Zigbee or Z-Wave logo on a smart bulb or lock box
is: Low-power smart-home mesh radios and the Matter standard that runs over them.
anchor: What are Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread and Matter?

see: A small box with a stubby antenna on a meter, fence or bin labeled LoRaWAN
is: A long-range, low-data-rate IoT sensor, at 915 MHz in the US.
anchor: What is LoRa, and how far does it reach?

see: A Helium crypto hotspot in a window
is: A crowd-built LoRaWAN gateway that earns tokens.
anchor: What is the Helium network, and is it legit?

see: A new digital electric meter with no spinning dial
is: An AMI smart meter that reports readings by radio, often a 902-928 MHz mesh.
anchor: What is that new electric meter, and does it transmit?

see: A letter from Eversource scheduling a meter swap
is: Eversource's Massachusetts smart meter rollout, due to finish by late 2027.
anchor: When is Eversource installing smart meters in Massachusetts?

see: A National Grid notice about a new meter
is: National Grid's Massachusetts smart meter rollout, with a fee-based opt-out.
anchor: Can I opt out of a National Grid smart meter in Massachusetts?

see: The amber horseshoe-shaped tire warning light on my dashboard
is: The TPMS warning, fed by 315 or 434 MHz sensors in each wheel.
anchor: What frequency do tire pressure sensors use?

see: The four curved lines of the contactless symbol
is: A 13.56 MHz tap-range link powered by the reader.
anchor: How does tap-to-pay work, and how close do I need to be?

see: A green CharlieCard or an MBTA gate that takes my phone
is: MBTA fare media: MIFARE Classic CharlieCard since 2006, contactless bank cards since August 2024.
anchor: Is the CharlieCard being replaced?

see: A gray toll tag behind the rearview mirror
is: An E-ZPass active RFID transponder at 915 MHz.
anchor: How does E-ZPass work?

see: A highway sign showing minutes to the next town
is: Travel times computed by matching Bluetooth MAC addresses at roadside readers.
anchor: How do highway signs know the travel time?

see: A presenter with a belt-pack transmitter and no mic cable
is: A wireless mic, a low-power transmitter sharing leftover TV spectrum
anchor: Who is allowed to put a microphone on the air?

see: A singer wearing a molded earpiece on stage
is: An in-ear monitor, a wireless transmitter sending the performer their mix
anchor: Who is allowed to put a microphone on the air?

see: A "50 mW" notice in a wireless mic manual
is: The US power cap for unlicensed mics in the TV bands
anchor: What is the 50 mW rule?

see: A cheap secondhand mic system labeled 700-something MHz
is: A 700 MHz mic, banned in the US since 2010
anchor: What happened to 700 MHz wireless microphones?

see: A wireless mic receiver tuned between 617 and 698 MHz
is: A 600 MHz mic that had to stop operating in the US by July 13, 2020
anchor: Is my 600 MHz wireless mic illegal?

see: Referees and coaches all on wireless at an NFL game
is: Hundreds of coordinated frequencies managed by SBE/NFL volunteers
anchor: Who coordinates frequencies at the Super Bowl?

see: A small antenna box on a lighting truss
is: Probably wireless DMX lighting control on 2.4 GHz
anchor: What about wireless lighting control?

see: A license plate like W1ABC on a car with a tall antenna
is: Likely a ham radio operator's call sign
anchor: What is a ham, and how do you become one in the US?

see: A UK call sign starting M7, M8, M9 or M0
is: A UK amateur licence; the prefix shows the licence level
anchor: What are the UK amateur radio licence levels?

see: A flyer for a radio "swapfest" in Cambridge
is: The MIT Swapfest, run by the MIT Radio Society W1MX
anchor: Are there ham radio clubs in Boston?

see: A USB stick with an antenna showing a rainbow waterfall on a laptop
is: An RTL-SDR, a cheap receive-only software-defined radio
anchor: What is a software-defined radio, and what is an RTL-SDR?

see: A flight tracker map with planes over my house
is: Aircraft ADS-B position broadcasts, receivable with an SDR
anchor: What can I listen to with an RTL-SDR?

see: A creepy buzzing shortwave station on YouTube
is: UVB-76 "The Buzzer" on 4625 kHz
anchor: What is UVB-76, "The Buzzer"?

see: A SAR number in my phone's legal settings
is: How much RF energy the phone deposits in tissue, tested against FCC or ICNIRP limits
anchor: What is the SAR limit for cell phones in the US?

see: Different SAR limits for the same phone in the US and Europe
is: Different averaging masses: 1.6 W/kg over 1 g (FCC) vs 2 W/kg over 10 g (ICNIRP)
anchor: Why is the US limit 1.6 and Europe's 2.0?

see: A headline saying WHO says phones may cause cancer
is: IARC's 2011 Group 2B classification, based on limited evidence
anchor: What does "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B) mean?

see: A post claiming 5G masts make people sick
is: WHO says no adverse health effect has been causally linked to wireless technologies
anchor: Is 5G dangerous to health?

see: Tall towers near Route 128 in Needham
is: Boston's TV antenna farm: WBZ-TV's Cedar Street tower and the Cabot Street candelabra.
anchor: Where do Boston TV stations broadcast from?

see: A tower whose top splits into several arms
is: A candelabra tower, holding a separate antenna for each TV station.
anchor: What is the stainless-steel tower with arms in Needham?

see: A mast on top of the Prudential
is: An FM broadcast mast with a shared master antenna (as of 2004).
anchor: What antennas are on top of the Prudential?

see: WBZ 1030 coming in from hundreds of miles away at night
is: A 50 kW clear-channel AM station whose night skywave travels far.
anchor: Why can I hear WBZ 1030 at night in other states?

see: Two bare towers by the water in Hull
is: WBZ's directional AM array, aimed at Boston and away from the Atlantic.
anchor: Where is WBZ's transmitter?

see: My phone works in the subway tunnel
is: A distributed antenna system carries carrier signals over fiber and leaky cable.
anchor: How does cell service reach the T tunnels?

see: Radios on MBTA staff and Transit Police
is: The MBTA is replacing EDACS with an L3Harris P25 system.
anchor: What radio do MBTA crews and Transit Police use?

see: Boston police and fire radio on a scanner app
is: A UHF P25 system being upgraded across ten city radio sites.
anchor: What radio system do Boston police and firefighters use?

see: Planes flying low over my house in Somerville or Milton
is: Logan runway use and satellite-guided RNAV paths concentrate tracks.
anchor: Why are planes flying over my house in Somerville, Cambridge or Milton?

see: A flight tracker showing a plane over Boston
is: Massport runs a near-live public Flight Monitor for Logan traffic.
anchor: How can I tell which plane just flew over Boston?

see: A ship-tracking website showing a tanker in the harbor
is: Ships broadcast position and identity on AIS, on dedicated marine VHF channels.
anchor: How do I track ships in Boston Harbor?

see: A new Eversource meter on my house
is: An Itron smart meter that reports usage daily by radio.
anchor: What is the new meter on my house, and can I opt out?

see: A Christmas Eve transmission on 486 kHz
is: WA1ZMS's experimental-license commemoration of Fessenden's claimed 1906 broadcast.
anchor: Was the first radio broadcast really from Brant Rock in 1906?

see: A Marconi marker on a Cape Cod bluff
is: The site of Marconi's 1903 Wellfleet transatlantic station.
anchor: Where was Marconi's station on Cape Cod?

see: A cluster of towers on a hill
is: An antenna farm, where stations share height, land and backup.
anchor: What is an antenna farm?

see: A very tall tower held up by cables
is: A guyed tower.
anchor: How do I tell a guyed tower from a candelabra?

see: Several identical bare towers in a row
is: An AM directional array; the towers themselves are the antenna.
anchor: Why do AM stations use several tall towers?

see: Stacked rectangular panels on a rooftop mast
is: Often FM broadcast panel antennas, though cell panels look similar.
anchor: What are the flat panels on a rooftop mast?

see: A thick cable along a subway tunnel wall
is: Radiating (leaky feeder) cable from a distributed antenna system.
anchor: What carries cell signals into a tunnel?

see: Who owns that tower?
is: Look it up free in the FCC's ASR database by coordinates and radius.
anchor: How do I look up a tower near me?

see: Who is licensed to transmit from that antenna?
is: Search the FCC's Universal Licensing System.
anchor: How do I find out who holds a radio license?
